tool.name: re
tool.tagline: Regular expressions for searching, validating, extracting and rewriting text
tool.description: The re module implements Perl-style regular expressions for Python strings and bytes. You use it to find patterns in text, validate formats, pull structured fields out of logs or documents, split on complex separators and perform rule-based replacements. Knowing it well also means knowing its limits: readability, Unicode details and catastrophic backtracking.

glossary.def: The part of Python's re module that takes your pattern and actually searches the text with it, trying positions and options one by one.

What re.search and the other re functions return when they find something: an object holding the matched text, where it was found, and the text of each group. When nothing is found you get None instead.
What re.compile returns: a regular expression prepared once, with its own search, findall, sub and other methods so you can reuse it.
In re: read a pattern once and turn it into an internal list of steps the regex engine can follow quickly. re.compile does it explicitly; the other re functions do it for you behind the scenes.
A character with a special meaning in a regular expression, such as . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | ^ $ or \. Put a backslash in front to match it as an ordinary character.
A set of characters in square brackets, like [aeiou] or [0-9], that matches exactly one character from the set. [^...] matches any one character that is not in it.
A part of a regex that matches a position rather than a character, such as ^ (start of the text), $ (end of the text) or \b (edge of a word).
The regex \b: the position where a word character (letter, digit or underscore) meets anything else, such as a space, punctuation or the start or end of the text.
A symbol after part of a regex saying how many times it may repeat: * (zero or more), + (one or more), ? (zero or one) or {m,n} (between m and n times).
Choosing between options with | in a regular expression: cat|dog matches cat or dog.
A quantifier's normal behaviour: take as many characters as possible, and give some back only if the rest of the pattern can't match otherwise.
A quantifier followed by ?, such as *? or +?, which takes as few characters as possible and grows only when the rest of the pattern needs it.
A part of a regex in parentheses whose matched text is remembered, so code can read it afterwards as group 1, group 2 and so on.
A group written (?:...) that bundles part of a regex, for example so a quantifier applies to all of it, without remembering the text it matched.
A capturing group given a name with (?P<name>...), so code can read its text by name instead of by number.
\1 (or (?P=name)) inside a regex: it matches exactly the same text that an earlier group captured, such as a repeated word.
A switch that changes how a whole regular expression matches, such as re.IGNORECASE to ignore upper and lower case. Several can be combined with |.
How Python's regex engine works: it tries one way of matching, and when that fails it goes back to its last choice and tries the next option.
A regex check of what comes right after (lookahead) or right before (lookbehind) the current position, without including that text in the match.
Converting text to a form where upper- and lower-case letters compare equal, used for case-insensitive matching. It is a little more thorough than lower().
The number Unicode assigns to one character; é is code point U+00E9. Some characters you see on screen are made of several code points.
Rewriting text so that characters that look the same are also stored the same way, for example é as one code point instead of e plus a separate accent.
When reading a small language or format: one meaningful piece of the input with a type attached, such as the number 42, the name x or the operator >=.
Code that cuts text into tokens (numbers, names, operators...) one after another, usually the first step of reading a small language or file format.
When a regex can match the same text in a huge number of ways and the match then fails, so the engine tries them all and can run for minutes or years on a short input.
Regular expression denial of service: an attack that sends text which makes a vulnerable regex run for a very long time, freezing the program.
A quantifier followed by +, such as *+ or ++ (Python 3.11+): it takes as much as it can and never gives any of it back.
A group written (?>...) (Python 3.11+): once it has matched, the regex engine won't go back and try matching it differently.
One small instruction, like 'match this letter' or 'repeat this part', in the list of steps an engine follows. re turns each pattern into such a list.

concepts.name: search, match and fullmatch
concepts.summary: Find a pattern anywhere with re.search, at the start with re.match, or require the whole string with re.fullmatch.
concepts.why: Picking the right one is the difference between an input check that works and one that lets bad values through.
concepts.body:
Say you want every order number in an email, or to check that someone typed a date like 2025-03-01. `in` and `startswith` only find fixed text. A **regular expression** (regex for short) describes the *shape* of text instead: `\d+` means "one or more digits", whatever the digits are. Python's built-in `re` module searches text with these patterns.

Three functions differ only in *where* the pattern has to fit:
- `re.search(pattern, text)` finds the **first** match anywhere in the text.
- `re.match(pattern, text)` only matches at the very **start** of the text.
- `re.fullmatch(pattern, text)` requires the pattern to cover the **entire** text. Use it to check that input has the right form.

When it finds something, each function returns a **Match object**: an object holding the matched text and where it was found. When nothing matches you get `None`, so check before using the result:

```python
m = re.search(r"\d+", "Order 1234")
if m:
    print(m.group())   # 1234
```

`m.group()` (or `m[0]`) is the matched text, and `m.start()`, `m.end()` and `m.span()` give its position as indexes into the string.

Notice the `r` before the quotes. It makes a **raw string**: Python keeps every backslash exactly as you typed it. In a normal string Python turns backslash codes into special characters first (as `\n` becomes a newline), so `"\b"` would turn into an invisible backspace character before `re` ever saw it. Always write patterns as raw strings.

Letters and digits in a pattern match themselves; the characters `. ^ $ * + ? { } [ ] \ | ( )` have special meanings, covered in the next lessons. For fixed text you don't need regex at all: `"abc" in text`, `text.startswith(...)` and `text.split(...)` are simpler and faster.
concepts.code:
import re

text = "Order 1234 shipped on 2025-03-01"

m = re.search(r"\d+", text)
print(m.group(), m.span())               # 1234 (6, 10)
print(re.match(r"\d+", text))            # None: text starts with 'O'
print(re.match(r"Order", text) is not None)   # True

# bool(...) turns a Match into True and None into False

for candidate in ["2025", "2025a", "x2025"]:
    print(candidate, bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", candidate)))
# 2025 True
# 2025a False
# x2025 False

# a normal string turns \b into one backspace character;
# a raw string keeps the backslash and the b
print(len("\b"), len(r"\b"))   # 1 2
takeaways: `search` anywhere, `match` at the start, `fullmatch` the whole string
They return a Match object or None; test the result before using it
Always write patterns as raw strings: r'...'
pitfalls: Using `re.match` to check input; it accepts any string that merely begins with a valid value.

quiz.q: Which call returns a match for the text 'id: 42'?
quiz.explain: Only search scans past the start; match and fullmatch both require the digits at position 0.

concepts.name: Characters, classes and anchors
concepts.summary: Use ., character classes like [a-z] and \d, and anchors such as ^, $ and \b to describe what to match and where.
concepts.why: Character classes and anchors are the vocabulary of every pattern you'll write.
concepts.body:
A pattern is read one piece at a time, and most pieces match exactly one character. A plain letter matches itself. A `.` (dot) matches any single character except a newline.

Square brackets make a **character class**: a set of characters, exactly one of which must appear. `[aeiou]` matches one vowel. Ranges work too, so `[a-z0-9]` is any lowercase letter or digit. A `^` right after the opening bracket flips the set: `[^aeiou]` is any character *except* a vowel. Inside brackets most special characters are ordinary, so `[.]` matches a real dot.

Some sets are so common they have shortcuts: `\d` a digit, `\w` a word character (letter, digit or underscore), `\s` whitespace. The capital versions `\D`, `\W`, `\S` mean the opposite. To match a special character itself, put a backslash in front: `\.` `\$` `\(`.

An **anchor** matches a *position* between characters rather than a character:
- `^` the start of the text, `$` the end.
- `\b` a **word boundary**: the edge of a word, where a word character meets a non-word character or the start or end of the text. `r"\bcat\b"` matches "cat" but not "category".
- `\A` and `\Z` are a strict start and end.

A subtle point: `$` also matches just **before a newline at the very end**, so `re.search(r"^\d+$", "123\n")` succeeds. When checking input, use `re.fullmatch` or end the pattern with `\Z`.

Python strings can hold characters from every language, because Python follows **Unicode**, the worldwide standard that gives each character a number. So `\d` also matches Arabic-Indic digits like ١٢٣, and `\w` matches letters like é or 東. Write `[0-9]` when you mean only the ten digits 0 to 9.
concepts.code:
import re

# re.findall(pattern, text) returns a list of every match (more on it later)
print(re.findall(r"\bcat\b", "cat category bobcat cat."))  # ['cat', 'cat']
print(re.findall(r"[aeiou]", "regex"))                     # ['e', 'e']
print(re.findall(r"[^a-z ]", "abc D3f!"))                  # ['D', '3', '!']
print(re.findall(r"\d\.\d", "v1.2 or 3x4"))                # ['1.2']
print(re.findall(r"\s", "a b\tc"))                         # [' ', '\t']

print(bool(re.search(r"^\d+$", "123\n")))     # True: $ before final \n
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d+", "123\n")))    # False
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d+", "١٢٣")))      # True: Unicode digits
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+", "١٢٣")))    # False
takeaways: `[...]` matches one character from a set; `[^...]` matches one character not in it
`\d` and `\w` also match digits and letters from other alphabets; use `[0-9]` for plain 0-9
`$` matches before a trailing newline; check whole input with fullmatch or `\Z`
pitfalls: Writing `.` to mean a real dot: `r'example.com'` also matches 'exampleXcom'. Write `r'example\.com'`.

quiz.q: Which pattern matches 'log' as a whole word in 'log logs catalog' only once?
quiz.explain: Word boundaries on both sides exclude 'logs' and 'catalog'.

concepts.name: Quantifiers and alternation
concepts.summary: Repeat parts of a pattern with *, +, ?, {m,n} and choose between alternatives with |.
concepts.why: Real data varies in length, and quantifiers are how patterns flex to fit it.
concepts.body:
A **quantifier** says how many times the item just before it may repeat. The item can be one character, a character class or a group in parentheses:
- `*` zero or more
- `+` one or more
- `?` zero or one (optional)
- `{3}` exactly three, `{2,4}` two to four, `{2,}` two or more

So `r"\d{3}-\d{4}"` matches `555-1234`, and `r"colou?r"` matches both spellings.

To repeat more than one character, wrap them in parentheses: `r"(ha)+"` matches `hahaha`, while `r"ha+"` matches `haaa`.

**Alternation**, the `|` sign, means "this or that": `r"cat|dog"` matches either word. It splits the *whole* pattern unless it is inside parentheses, so `r"^cat|dog$"` means `^cat` *or* `dog$`. Write `r"^(cat|dog)$"` to anchor the whole choice.

Alternatives are tried left to right, and the first one that leads to an overall match wins. So when one alternative is the beginning of another, put the longer one first (`r"https|http"`).

Quantifiers are **greedy**: they take as many characters as they can, and give some back only if the rest of the pattern would otherwise fail. That matters most with `.*` ("anything, any number of times"), which gets its own lesson later.

Be careful with `*`: a pattern like `r"\d*"` happily matches zero characters, the empty string, which can give surprising results with `search` or `findall`.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"\d{3}-\d{4}", "call 555-1234 or 555-98765"))  # ['555-1234', '555-9876']
print(re.findall(r"colou?r", "color colour colouur"))        # ['color', 'colour']
print(re.fullmatch(r"(ha)+", "hahaha") is not None)          # True
print(re.fullmatch(r"ha+", "hahaha") is not None)            # False
print(re.findall(r"\b\w{5,}\b", "a quick brown fox jumps"))  # ['quick', 'brown', 'jumps']

print(re.search(r"http|https", "https://x").group())         # http
print(re.search(r"https?", "https://x").group())             # https
print(re.search(r"\d*", "abc123").group() == "")            # True: empty match at 0
takeaways: `* + ? {m,n}` repeat the item before them; use parentheses to repeat several characters
`|` splits the whole pattern; put the choice in parentheses before anchoring it
`*` and `?` allow empty matches, which can surprise you
pitfalls: Writing `^a|b$` and expecting both alternatives to be anchored at both ends.

quiz.q: What does re.findall(r'ab+', 'ab abbb a b') return?
quiz.explain: + applies only to b, so each match is an a followed by one or more b's.

concepts.name: Capturing groups
concepts.summary: Capture parts of a match with parentheses and read them with group(n) and groups().
concepts.why: Pulling out pieces such as the year of a date, an ID or the two halves of a name=value pair is the main reason to use regex.
concepts.body:
Parentheses do two jobs. They **group** items so a quantifier or `|` applies to all of them, and they **capture**: they remember the text their part matched. A pair of parentheses is called a **capturing group**.

Groups are numbered by their opening parenthesis from left to right, starting at 1:

```python
m = re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", "due 2025-03-01")
m.group(1)   # '2025'
m.groups()   # ('2025', '03', '01')
```

`m.group(0)` is the whole match; `m.group(1, 3)` returns a tuple of several groups. A group that took no part in the match (for example inside an optional `(...)?`) gives `None`.

If you need parentheses only for grouping, write a **non-capturing group** `(?:...)`. It is skipped in the numbering, which keeps it simple: `r"(?:https?://)?(\w+\.com)"` captures only the site name.

Groups also change what other functions return, which surprises people: `re.findall` returns the group's text instead of the whole match when the pattern has groups, and `re.split` includes captured separators in its result.

Inside the pattern, `\1` matches the exact text that group 1 matched. This is a **backreference**, so `r"\b(\w+) \1\b"` finds doubled words like "the the".
concepts.code:
import re

m = re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", "due 2025-03-01, paid")
print(m.group(0))            # 2025-03-01
print(m.group(1), m[2])      # 2025 03
print(m.groups())            # ('2025', '03', '01')
year = int(m.group(1))       # groups are strings; convert to use as numbers
print(year + 1)              # 2026

m = re.search(r"(?:https?://)?([\w.]+\.com)(/\S*)?", "see example.com now")
print(m.groups())            # ('example.com', None)

print(re.search(r"\b(\w+) \1\b", "it was the the end").group(1))  # the
takeaways: Each `( )` captures; numbering follows the opening parentheses
Use `(?:...)` when you only need grouping
Groups that didn't take part in the match return None
pitfalls: Adding a capturing group to a pattern used with findall and suddenly getting only the group's text back.

quiz.explain: The optional group 2 did not participate, so it is None while numbering stays fixed.

concepts.name: findall, finditer and split
concepts.summary: Collect every match with findall or finditer, and split strings on patterns with re.split.
concepts.why: Pulling all numbers, emails or words out of text, and splitting on messy separators, are everyday jobs.
concepts.body:
`re.findall(pattern, text)` returns all matches as a list. What goes in the list depends on the groups:
- with **no groups**, the matched strings;
- with **one group**, that group's text;
- with **several groups**, a tuple of group texts per match.

`re.finditer` hands you the Match objects one at a time instead of a list, for use in a `for` loop. Use it when you need positions, or both the whole match and its parts. On big texts it also saves memory, since it never builds the full list.

`re.split(pattern, text)` splits on every match of the pattern, where `str.split` only handles one fixed separator:

```python
re.split(r"[,;\s]+", "a, b;c  d")   # ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
```

If the pattern contains a capturing group, the separators are **included** in the result. That's handy for splitting a sum like `3+4-1` into numbers and signs, but surprising otherwise; use `(?:...)` to avoid it. `maxsplit=` limits the number of splits.

Since Python 3.13, giving `maxsplit` by position is **deprecated**: it still works but prints a warning and will be removed later. Write `re.split(p, s, maxsplit=1)`, not `re.split(p, s, 1)`; the name also makes the call easier to read.

Matches never overlap: after a match, scanning continues where it ended.
concepts.code:
import re

log = "ERROR 12ms user=ann; WARN 7ms user=bob; ERROR 30ms user=cy"
print(re.findall(r"\d+ms", log))              # ['12ms', '7ms', '30ms']
print(re.findall(r"(\d+)ms", log))            # ['12', '7', '30']
print(re.findall(r"(\w+) (\d+)ms", log)[:2])  # [('ERROR', '12'), ('WARN', '7')]

for m in re.finditer(r"user=(\w+)", log):
    print(m.group(1), m.start())
# ann 11
# bob 30
# cy 51

print(re.split(r"[,;\s]+", "a, b;c  d"))       # ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']
print(re.split(r"([+-])", "3+4-1"))            # ['3', '+', '4', '-', '1']
print(re.split(r"\s+", "a b c", maxsplit=1))   # ['a', 'b c']
takeaways: findall returns strings, group texts or tuples depending on the groups
finditer gives Match objects one by one, with their positions
re.split includes captured separators; pass `maxsplit=` by name
pitfalls: Writing `re.split(p, s, 1)`; pass `maxsplit=1` by name, since the positional form is deprecated in 3.13.

quiz.explain: With two groups, findall returns a tuple of group texts for each match.

concepts.name: Named groups and Match objects
concepts.summary: Name your groups with (?P<name>...) and use groupdict, span and lastgroup to work with matches cleanly.
concepts.why: Named groups make complex patterns self-documenting and turn matches straight into dicts.
concepts.body:
Numbered groups get confusing once a pattern has more than two or three. **Named groups** fix that:

```python
pat = r"(?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<ms>\d+)ms"
```

Read them by name with `m.group("level")` or `m["level"]`, or all at once with `m.groupdict()`, which returns a dict of name to text, ready to store or save as JSON. `groupdict(default="")` puts `""` instead of `None` for groups that didn't match. Named groups still have numbers too.

Inside the pattern, refer back to a named group with `(?P=name)`; in `re.sub` replacements use `\g<name>`.

Match objects carry more than text:
- `m.start("ms")`, `m.end()`, `m.span("level")` give positions per group
- `m.lastgroup` is the name of the last group that matched, handy when a pattern has several named alternatives and you need to know which one fired
- `m.re` and `m.string` are the pattern and the input
- `m.expand(r"...")` builds a string from a replacement like the ones `re.sub` takes

A Match object always counts as true, which is why `if m:` works.

Combining `finditer` and `groupdict` is the most readable way to turn lines with a fixed layout, such as the timestamped log lines programs write as they run, into dictionaries.
concepts.code:
import re

LINE = re.compile(r"(?P<time>\d\d:\d\d) (?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<msg>.*)")
log = "10:01 INFO started\n10:02 ERROR disk full\n10:05 INFO done"

records = [m.groupdict() for m in LINE.finditer(log)]
print(records[1])    # {'time': '10:02', 'level': 'ERROR', 'msg': 'disk full'}

m = LINE.search(log)
print(m["level"], m.span("msg"))       # INFO (11, 18)
print(m.expand(r"[\g<level>] \g<msg>"))  # [INFO] started

pair = re.compile(r"(?P<q>['\"])(?P<body>.*?)(?P=q)")
print(pair.search("say 'hi' or \"yo\"")["body"])   # hi
takeaways: `(?P<name>...)` names a group; read it with `m['name']` or `m.groupdict()`
`(?P=name)` matches the same text again inside the pattern
`m.span(name)` and `m.lastgroup` describe where and what matched

quiz.explain: The v group participates and matches the empty string, so its value is '' rather than None.

concepts.name: Replacing with sub
concepts.summary: Rewrite text with re.sub using backreferences, named groups and replacement functions.
concepts.why: Cleaning up data, hiding private details such as card numbers and reformatting dates are all pattern-based replacements.
concepts.body:
`re.sub(pattern, repl, text)` replaces every match with `repl` and returns the new string. `count=1` limits the number of replacements; `re.subn` also returns how many were made.

The replacement string can refer to groups:
- `\1`, `\2` insert the text of numbered groups (use a raw string: `r"\2/\1"`).
- `\g<name>` inserts a named group, and `\g<1>` avoids ambiguity before digits (`\g<1>0` vs `\10`).
- Other backslash codes in `repl` are processed too, so a real backslash must be written `\\`.

Instead of a string, `repl` can be a **function** that receives the Match object and returns the replacement. Use it when the replacement needs logic: converting units, looking up values in a dict, changing case:

```python
re.sub(r"\d+", lambda m: str(int(m[0]) * 2), "3 apples")
```

When the replacement text comes from users or data, either double its backslashes or use a function returning the text, so sequences like `\1` in the data aren't treated as group references.

Since 3.13, pass `count` by name (`count=1`); passing it by position is deprecated.

For fixed text, `str.replace` is simpler and faster.
concepts.code:
import re

dates = "from 03/01/2025 to 12/31/2025"
print(re.sub(r"(\d{2})/(\d{2})/(\d{4})", r"\3-\1-\2", dates))
# from 2025-03-01 to 2025-12-31

print(re.sub(r"(?P<user>\w+)@(\w+)\.com", r"\g<user>@***", "mail ann@corp.com"))
# mail ann@***

prices = {"apple": 0.5, "pear": 0.75}
order = "3 apple, 2 pear"
total = re.sub(r"(\d+) (\w+)", lambda m: f"{int(m[1]) * prices[m[2]]:.2f}", order)
print(total)                                           # 1.50, 1.50

text, n = re.subn(r"\s+", " ", "too   many \t spaces")
print(text, n)                                         # too many spaces 2
print(re.sub(r"x", "y", "xxx", count=1))               # yxx
takeaways: `\1` and `\g<name>` insert groups in the replacement; use raw strings
A function as `repl` computes each replacement from the Match
Pass `count=` by name; by position is deprecated since 3.13
pitfalls: Inserting user data as the replacement string, where backslashes are interpreted as group references.

quiz.q: What does re.sub(r'(\w+) (\w+)', r'\2 \1', 'hello world') return?
quiz.explain: The replacement swaps the two captured groups.

concepts.name: Flags, compile and verbose patterns
concepts.summary: Change matching behaviour with IGNORECASE, MULTILINE, DOTALL and VERBOSE, and precompile patterns with re.compile.
concepts.why: Flags fix the most common 'why doesn't it match' problems, and verbose mode keeps long patterns maintainable.
concepts.body:
A **regex flag** is a switch that changes how a whole pattern matches. Pass flags as `flags=` and combine several with `|`:
- `re.IGNORECASE` (`re.I`) ignores upper and lower case.
- `re.MULTILINE` (`re.M`) makes `^` and `$` match at the start and end of **every line**, not just of the whole text.
- `re.DOTALL` (`re.S`) makes `.` match newlines too.
- `re.VERBOSE` (`re.X`) ignores spaces and line breaks in the pattern and allows `#` comments, so you can lay out a long pattern over several lines. Write a real space as `\ ` or `[ ]`.
- `re.ASCII` (`re.A`) makes `\w`, `\d`, `\s` and `\b` cover only **ASCII**, the basic set of English letters, digits 0-9 and common symbols.

Flags can also be written at the very start of the pattern, `(?i)`, `(?m)`, `(?x)`, or for one part only: `(?i:abc)def`.

`re.compile(pattern, flags)` **compiles** the pattern: it reads and prepares it once, and returns a **Pattern object** with the same methods (`search`, `findall`, `sub`...). The plain `re.search`-style functions keep recently compiled patterns in a **cache**, a stash of results kept for reuse, so compiling yourself isn't mainly about speed. It helps readability: define named patterns once at the top of a file. Pattern methods also take `pos` and `endpos` to search only part of the text.

Always pass flags by name. Since 3.13, giving `count`, `maxsplit` or `flags` to `sub`, `subn` and `split` by position triggers a `DeprecationWarning`, and it hid real bugs: `re.split(p, s, re.I)` silently meant `maxsplit=2`, because flags are numbers underneath.
concepts.code:
import re text = "Name: Ann\nname: Bob\nAGE: 31" print(re.findall(r"^name: (\w+)", text, flags=re.I | re.M)) # ['Ann', 'Bob'] print(re.findall(r"^name: (\w+)", text)) # [] html = "

one\ntwo

" print(re.search(r"

(.*)

", html)) # None print(repr(re.search(r"

(.*)

", html, re.S).group(1))) # 'one\ntwo' PHONE = re.compile(r""" \(?(\d{3})\)? # area code, optional parentheses [\s.-]? # separator (\d{3})[\s.-]?(\d{4}) """, re.VERBOSE) print(PHONE.findall("(555) 123-4567 and 555.987.6543")) # [('555', '123', '4567'), ('555', '987', '6543')] print(PHONE.search("x 555 123 4567", pos=2).groups()) # ('555', '123', '4567')
takeaways: `re.I`, `re.M`, `re.S`, `re.X`, `re.A` change matching; combine with `|`
MULTILINE affects ^ and $; DOTALL affects .
`re.compile` gives reusable, well-named Pattern objects; VERBOSE allows comments
pitfalls: Forgetting that whitespace is ignored in VERBOSE mode, so a real space in the pattern silently disappears.

quiz.q: You search a multi-line string with r'^ERROR' but only the first line is checked. Which flag fixes it?
quiz.explain: MULTILINE makes ^ match at the beginning of every line.

concepts.name: Greedy vs lazy quantifiers
concepts.summary: Understand why .* overshoots, and use lazy quantifiers or negated character classes to match the shortest text.
concepts.why: Greedy matching is behind the classic 'my pattern swallowed everything' bug.
concepts.body: Quantifiers are greedy. To see what that costs, look at how matching works. The **regex engine**, the part of `re` that runs your pattern, lets `.*` grab everything up to the end of the text first. Then, if the rest of the pattern can't match, it **backtracks**: it gives back one character at a time and tries again. So on `bold and more`, the pattern `r".*"` matches from the first `` to the **last** ``. Adding `?` after a quantifier makes it a **lazy quantifier** (non-greedy): `*?`, `+?`, `??`, `{m,n}?`. It takes as little as possible and grows only when needed, so `r".*?"` matches each bold part separately. Often a negated character class is better than a lazy `.*?`: `r"[^<]*"` states exactly what may appear inside, can't run past the closing tag, and backtracks less. Similarly, `r'"[^"]*"'` matches a quoted string. A lazy quantifier doesn't find the shortest possible match in the whole text. The engine still returns the **leftmost** match, then makes it as short as it can from that starting point. Python 3.11 added **possessive** quantifiers (`*+`, `++`, `?+`) and `(?>...)` groups, which never give back what they matched. Both are covered in the backtracking lesson. For web pages (HTML), use a proper HTML reader such as the built-in `html.parser` or BeautifulSoup: tags nest and vary in ways a regex quietly gets wrong. Regex is fine for quick extraction from small, predictable snippets.
concepts.code: import re s = "bold and more" print(re.findall(r".*", s)) # ['bold and more'] print(re.findall(r".*?", s)) # ['bold', 'more'] print(re.findall(r"([^<]*)", s)) # ['bold', 'more'] q = 'say "hi" then "bye"' print(re.findall(r'"(.*)"', q)) # ['hi" then "bye'] print(re.findall(r'"([^"]*)"', q)) # ['hi', 'bye'] print(re.search(r"a+?", "aaa").group()) # a print(re.search(r"x.*?y", "xaxby").group()) # xaxby (leftmost wins)
takeaways: Greedy quantifiers take as much as possible, then backtrack
Add `?` for a lazy quantifier: `.*?`, `+?`
Negated character classes like `[^<]*` are clearer and faster than lazy dots
pitfalls: Using `.*` between two markers (quotes, tags, brackets) on text that contains several marked parts.

quiz.explain: The greedy .* runs to the last closing parenthesis.

concepts.name: Lookahead and lookbehind
concepts.summary: Check what comes before or after a position without including it in the match, using (?=...), (?!...), (?<=...) and (?<!...).
concepts.why: Lookarounds express conditions like 'a number followed by px' or 'a password containing a digit' cleanly.
concepts.body:
Sometimes you want a condition on the surroundings of a match without making the surroundings part of it: "the number before `px`", but not the `px`. A **lookaround** checks text right after or right before the current position and then matches nothing itself. Like anchors, it matches a position, not characters.

- `(?=...)` lookahead: what follows must match.
- `(?!...)` negative lookahead: what follows must not match.
- `(?<=...)` lookbehind: what precedes must match.
- `(?<!...)` negative lookbehind: what precedes must not match.

Examples:
- `r"\d+(?=px)"` matches the number in `12px` but not the unit.
- `r"(?<=\$)\d+"` matches amounts after a dollar sign.
- `r"\b(?!test_)\w+\.py\b"` matches Python files not starting with `test_`.
- Several lookaheads at the start test separate conditions on the same text: `r"^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,}$"` requires a digit, an uppercase letter and a length of 8 or more.

Python requires a lookbehind to be **fixed width**: everything inside must always match the same number of characters. `(?<=\$|USD )` fails because the alternatives differ in length (write `(?:(?<=\$)|(?<=USD ))` instead), and quantifiers like `+` aren't allowed inside. The third-party `regex` module lifts that restriction.

Lookarounds shine in `re.sub`, because they let you insert text at a position: `re.sub(r"(?<=\d)(?=(?:\d{3})+$)", ",", "1234567")` adds thousands separators.

Readability suffers quickly; when a condition is easier as a second check in plain Python, write the second check.
concepts.code:
import re

print(re.findall(r"\d+(?=px)", "w: 12px; h: 30em; m: 4px"))   # ['12', '4']
print(re.findall(r"(?<=\$)\d+", "cost $40, tax 5, tip $6"))   # ['40', '6']
print(re.findall(r"\b(?!test_)\w+\.py\b", "app.py test_app.py db.py"))
# ['app.py', 'db.py']

strong = re.compile(r"^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,}$")
for pw in ["password1", "Password1", "Pass1"]:
    print(pw, bool(strong.match(pw)))
# password1 False
# Password1 True
# Pass1 False

print(re.sub(r"(?<=\d)(?=(?:\d{3})+$)", ",", "1234567"))  # 1,234,567
try:
    re.compile(r"(?<=\$|USD )\d+")
except re.error as e:
    print(e)        # look-behind requires fixed-width pattern
takeaways: Lookarounds check the surroundings without including them in the match
Python lookbehind must be fixed width
Several lookaheads at one position test independent conditions
pitfalls: Writing a variable-width lookbehind such as `(?<=\s+)`, which raises re.error.

quiz.q: What does re.sub(r'(?<=a)b', 'X', 'ab cb ab') return?
quiz.explain: Only b's preceded by a are replaced, and the a itself is not part of the match.

concepts.name: Unicode, bytes and case folding
concepts.summary: Know how str and bytes patterns differ, what \w and IGNORECASE mean for Unicode, and when to use re.ASCII.
concepts.why: Text in many languages, and raw bytes such as file contents or network messages, break naive patterns in subtle ways.
concepts.body:
The re module works on both `str` and `bytes`, but the pattern and the text must be the same type: `re.search(rb"\d+", data)` for bytes, `r"\d+"` for strings. Mixing them raises `TypeError`.

In **str patterns**, matching follows Unicode by default:
- `\w` matches letters and digits from every alphabet, so `café` and `東京` are words; `\d` matches any Unicode decimal digit; `\s` includes non-breaking and other Unicode spaces.
- `re.IGNORECASE` compares the **case-folded** form of each character, a lower-case-like form designed for comparing. That brings surprises: the Kelvin sign `K` (U+212A) matches `k`, and `ſ` (long s) matches `s`. But folding that turns one character into two is not applied: `ß` does not match `ss`.
- `re.ASCII` limits `\w \d \s \b` (and ignoring case) to ASCII, which is what you want for things defined in plain ASCII, such as variable names, file formats and network messages.

In **bytes patterns**, everything is ASCII-only; bytes above 127 are never word characters.

Text that looks identical may be stored differently. Unicode numbers every character, and each number is a **code point**: `é` can be one code point (U+00E9) or `e` followed by a separate accent mark. **Unicode normalization** rewrites text into one standard form; run `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)` on both the pattern input and the text before matching what users type.

For characters on screen built from several code points (like many emoji), for selecting characters by alphabet such as `\p{Greek}`, or for folding `ß` to `ss`, use the third-party `regex` module.
concepts.code:
import re
import unicodedata

print(re.findall(r"\w+", "naïve café 東京"))          # ['naïve', 'café', '東京']
print(re.findall(r"\w+", "naïve café", re.ASCII))     # ['na', 've', 'caf']
print(re.findall(rb"\d+", b"id=42;len=7"))            # [b'42', b'7']

print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"k", "\u212a", re.I)))       # True: Kelvin sign
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"ss", "ß", re.I)))           # False

decomposed = "cafe\u0301"                             # e + combining accent
print(re.search(r"café", decomposed))                 # None
nfc = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", decomposed)
print(re.search(r"café", nfc) is not None)            # True
try:
    re.search(r"\d", b"1")
except TypeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                           # TypeError
takeaways: str patterns follow Unicode; bytes patterns are ASCII-only
Use `re.ASCII` for formats defined in plain ASCII, like variable names
Normalize text with unicodedata before matching what users type
pitfalls: Checking usernames with `\w+` and accidentally allowing look-alike letters from other alphabets.

quiz.q: Why might r'^\w+$' be a poor choice to validate ASCII-only usernames?
options: \w matches letters from any alphabet, like Cyrillic look-alikes
quiz.explain: In str patterns \w follows Unicode; add re.ASCII or use [A-Za-z0-9_].

concepts.name: Writing a tokenizer with regex
concepts.summary: Combine named alternatives into one master pattern and use finditer with lastgroup to tokenize input.
concepts.why: Any program that reads a small language, such as a settings format, a search-box syntax or a calculator, starts by cutting its input into tokens.
concepts.body:
A **tokenizer** cuts text into **tokens**: small pieces with a type attached, such as the number `2.5`, the name `x` or the operator `>=`. It is the first step in reading any little language. With re, the classic recipe from the Python docs is:

1. Write one named group per token type.
2. Join them with `|` into one master pattern, ordered so longer or more specific tokens come first (`>=` before `>`).
3. Loop with `finditer`; `m.lastgroup` tells you which alternative matched.
4. Add a catch-all group such as `MISMATCH=r"."` so unexpected characters are reported instead of silently skipped, and a `SKIP` group for whitespace.

Because `finditer` searches rather than matching back to back, an input character not covered by any alternative would be skipped. The catch-all closes that gap. Alternatively, call `pattern.match(text, pos)` in a loop, which pins each token to the current position.

Keep `m.start()` to produce error messages that point at the problem, and count newlines in `SKIP` or `NEWLINE` tokens to report line numbers.

For keywords such as `if`, match a general name and then look it up in a set of keywords. That's simpler, and avoids `if` being matched inside `iffy`.

The next step is a **parser**: code that reads the tokens and works out their structure, such as which numbers an operator applies to. Small parsers are easy to write by hand, one function per grammar rule; for a bigger language, use a parser library.
takeaways: Join named alternatives into one master pattern; `m.lastgroup` gives the token type
Order alternatives so longer operators come first
Add SKIP and MISMATCH groups so nothing is silently ignored
pitfalls: Omitting a catch-all group, so finditer silently skips characters no rule matches.

quiz.q: In the master pattern, why must '>=' come before '>' in the OP alternatives?
options: Alternatives are tried left to right, so '>' would match first and leave '=' as a separate token
quiz.explain: The first alternative that matches wins, so longer tokens must be listed first.

concepts.name: Catastrophic backtracking and ReDoS
concepts.summary: Recognise patterns that take exponential time, and fix them with tighter character classes, possessive quantifiers or atomic groups.
concepts.why: One bad pattern, fed text an attacker chose, can keep the processor busy for minutes: enough to take a service down.
concepts.body:
Python's re is a backtracking engine: when part of a pattern fails, it goes back and tries the other ways earlier quantifiers could have matched. Usually that's cheap. But with **nested or overlapping quantifiers**, the number of ways can grow exponentially with the input's length when the overall match fails. This is **catastrophic backtracking**.

Classic culprits:
- `(a+)+$` on `"aaaa...a!"`: the inner and outer `+` can split the run of a's in exponentially many ways.
- `(\w+\s?)+$`, `(.*,)*`, `(a|aa)+`: alternatives or repetitions that can match the same text in several ways.

Matching succeeds fast; it's the **failure** path that explodes. Each extra character can double the time. An attacker who controls the input can use this to freeze your program, an attack called **ReDoS** (regular expression denial of service).

Fixes:
- Make the pieces unable to match the same text: `[^,]*,` instead of `.*,`; drop the redundant inner quantifier (`a+$`).
- Use **possessive quantifiers** (`*+`, `++`, `?+`) or **atomic groups** `(?>...)`, available since Python 3.11. They match greedily and never give characters back, so there are no other ways left to try.
- Limit the input's length before matching.
- For text from strangers, consider an engine whose running time grows only in step with the input's length, such as the third-party `google-re2` package.

`re` has no time limit: a runaway match can't be interrupted from inside the program. The only way out is to run the match in a separate **process**, a second running copy of Python, and kill that process if it takes too long.
concepts.code:
import re
import time

def timed(pattern, text):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    result = re.match(pattern, text)
    return result is not None, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3)

evil = "a" * 24 + "!"
ok, slow = timed(r"(a+)+$", evil)
print(ok, slow > 0.05)                 # False True  (exponential)
ok, fast = timed(r"(?:a++)+$", evil)   # possessive inner quantifier
print(ok, fast < 0.01)                 # False True
ok, fast = timed(r"a+$", evil)         # just remove the nesting
print(ok, fast < 0.01)                 # False True

print(re.match(r"(?>a+)ab", "aaab"))   # None: atomic group gives nothing back
print(re.match(r"a+ab", "aaab"))       # <re.Match object; span=(0, 4), match='aaab'>
takeaways: Nested or overlapping quantifiers can make failing matches exponential
Possessive quantifiers and atomic groups (3.11+) remove backtracking
Limit input size, or use a linear-time engine, for text from strangers
pitfalls: Testing a pattern only on inputs that match; catastrophic cases show up on near-misses.

quiz.q: Why does re.match(r'(a+)+$', 'a' * 30 + '!') take so long?
options: The input is too long for the regex cache
The engine tries exponentially many ways to split the a's before concluding there's no match
quiz.explain: The nested quantifiers create overlapping choices that are all explored when the final $ fails.

concepts.name: How the re engine compiles and caches
concepts.summary: Look inside re: how patterns become opcodes, re.DEBUG output, the compiled-pattern cache and practical performance tips.
concepts.why: Knowing what the engine does explains which patterns are fast and how to debug confusing ones.
concepts.body:
`re.compile` works in three steps. It parses the pattern into a tree showing how the pieces nest (in `re._parser`). It turns that tree into a list of **opcodes**, small instructions like "match this letter" or "repeat this part". A fast matching engine written in C (`_sre`) then follows those instructions, and you get back a Pattern object.

Calls like `re.search(p, s)` look up `p` in an internal cache, keyed by pattern, type and flags, so repeated calls don't recompile. The cache holds a few hundred patterns. Programs that generate many different patterns push each other out and recompile constantly. Use `re.compile` for patterns built while the program runs or used in loops that run many times; `re.purge()` clears the cache.

Pass `re.DEBUG` to print the parse tree. It's a quick way to see how the pattern was really understood, for example whether `|` split where you thought.

Performance lessons from the engine's design:
- A pattern starting with fixed text, like `error: \d+`, lets the engine jump quickly to likely positions.
- Alternatives that are single characters (`a|e|i`) are turned into a character set automatically, but multi-character alternatives become a BRANCH whose arms are tried one by one at every position.
- An anchored pattern (`^`, `match`, `fullmatch`) fails quickly instead of retrying at every start position.
- Plain string methods (`in`, `startswith`, `str.replace`) beat regex for fixed text.

Python **threads** let one program work on several tasks at once, but they won't speed up heavy regex work on the standard build. The engine holds the **GIL**, a global lock that lets only one thread run Python code at a time, for the whole match. To run many matches at the same time, use separate processes (separate running copies of Python).
concepts.code:
import re
import timeit

re.compile(r"(?:a|e|i)+", re.DEBUG)
# MAX_REPEAT 1 MAXREPEAT
#   IN              <- single-char alternation became a set
#     LITERAL 97
#     LITERAL 101
#     LITERAL 105
# (followed by the compiled opcode listing)

text = "x" * 10_000 + "needle"
t_regex = timeit.timeit(lambda: re.search(r"needle", text), number=2000)
t_str = timeit.timeit(lambda: "needle" in text, number=2000)
print(t_str < t_regex)          # True: fixed text needs no regex

pats = [re.compile(fr"id{i}=(\d+)") for i in range(3)]   # compile dynamic ones once
print([p.search("id1=7").group(1) if p.search("id1=7") else None for p in pats])
# [None, '7', None]
takeaways: Patterns compile to opcodes for a C backtracking engine; results are cached
Compile patterns built at run time or used in busy loops explicitly; use `re.DEBUG` to inspect parsing
Patterns starting with fixed text, and anchored ones, are fast; multi-character alternatives are tried branch by branch
pitfalls: Generating thousands of different patterns while the program runs and relying on the module cache.

quiz.q: What does re.compile(r'(?:a|e|i|o|u)+', re.DEBUG) reveal about the alternation?
options: It stays a BRANCH tried arm by arm
It is compiled to a lookahead
Each vowel becomes a separate group
The parser turned it into a character set (IN), like [aeiou]
quiz.explain: The parser optimises alternatives that are all single characters into one set test.

concepts.name: Building patterns safely at runtime
concepts.summary: Build regexes from what users type or from word lists safely, with re.escape, longest-first alternation and size limits.
concepts.why: Unescaped input in a pattern is a correctness bug at best and a denial-of-service hole at worst.
concepts.body:
Patterns often come from data: a search box, a list of banned words, configurable rules. Three things go wrong.

**Escaping.** User text like `"1+1"` or `"C++"` contains **metacharacters**, characters with a special meaning in a pattern. `re.escape(s)` puts a backslash before everything special, so the text is matched exactly as typed. Never insert raw input into a pattern: a user could type `(a+)+$` and trigger catastrophic backtracking. Sneaking pattern syntax in this way is called regex injection.

**Alternation order.** When joining many words with `|`, the engine takes the first alternative that matches, not the longest. Sort by length, longest first (`sorted(words, key=len, reverse=True)`), so `"new york"` wins over `"new"`. Wrap the whole alternation in a group with word boundaries: `rf"\b(?:{alts})\b"`.

**Scale.** An alternation of 10,000 words becomes a branch the engine tries arm by arm at every position. For big word lists, it's faster to split the text into words with a simple pattern (`\w+`) and look each word up in a `set`, or to use a search method built for many words at once, such as the Aho-Corasick algorithm from a third-party package.

In replacement strings, escape backslashes too (`repl.replace("\\", "\\\\")`), or pass a function that returns the text unchanged.

If users really need to write patterns, cap their length, compile them inside try/except `re.error`, and run them only on input of limited size, ideally with an engine like `google-re2` whose time grows only with input length.
concepts.code:
import re

query = "C++ (beta)"
print(re.escape(query))                    # C\+\+\ \(beta\)
print(bool(re.search(re.escape(query), "Using C++ (beta) today")))  # True

cities = ["new", "new york", "york"]
naive = re.compile(r"\b(?:" + "|".join(map(re.escape, cities)) + r")\b")
print(naive.findall("I love new york"))    # ['new', 'york']
ordered = sorted(cities, key=len, reverse=True)
better = re.compile(r"\b(?:" + "|".join(map(re.escape, ordered)) + r")\b")
print(better.findall("I love new york"))   # ['new york']

banned = {"spam", "scam", "fraud"}
words = re.findall(r"\w+", "This is not a SCAM, honest".lower())
print([w for w in words if w in banned])   # ['scam']

try:
    re.compile("(unclosed")
except re.error as e:
    print(e.msg)                           # missing ), unterminated subpattern
takeaways: Always `re.escape` user text inserted into a pattern
Sort alternatives longest first; the first match wins, not the longest
For large word lists, split into words and use a set instead of one huge alternation
pitfalls: Building `re.compile(user_input)` directly, letting users inject slow or invalid patterns.

quiz.q: Why sort words by length before joining them with '|'?
options: The first alternative that matches wins, so a shorter prefix would shadow longer words
quiz.explain: Alternation is ordered; 'new' would match before 'new york' is tried.
